facts: Kruger records 147 mammal, 507 bird and 336 tree species — far more than just the Big Five.
The public network includes 12 main rest camps plus smaller bushveld, satellite and bush-lodge camps.
Fuel, food and basic supplies are available in the main camps, so a multi-day self-drive can stay entirely inside the park.
Around 690 rock-art sites preserve more than 35,000 images made across roughly four millennia.
The escarpment is a continental watershed: rivers run east to the Indian Ocean and west into the Senqu–Orange system.
The protected area shelters more than 250 endemic plant species as well as high-altitude wetlands above 2,750 metres.
Garden Route National Park is not one continuous reserve: it links the Wilderness lakes, Knysna forests and Tsitsikamma coast.
The classic Otter Trail covers 42 kilometres over five days and has six emergency escape routes.
At Storms River Mouth, a forest boardwalk reaches the suspension bridges without committing to a full-day hike.
Stellenbosch, founded in 1679, is South Africa’s second-oldest colonial town and a showcase of Cape Dutch architecture.
Franschhoek’s Huguenot story is woven into its farms, surnames and museum as much as into the wine labels.
Many estates pair tastings with gardens, art, hiking or restaurants, so non-drinkers can still build a full day here.
Hole in the Wall is a wave-cut opening in a coastal cliff and one of the region’s most recognisable natural landmarks.
Traditional Xhosa villages still sit between beaches and rolling grassland; this is a lived-in cultural landscape, not an empty wilderness.
Multi-day coastal walks involve tidal rivers and path-finding, so a local guide adds far more than navigation.
The park crosses the South Africa–Botswana border and protects about 38,000 square kilometres of Kalahari.
Wildlife concentrates along the dry Auob and Nossob riverbeds, where black-maned lions and raptors are signature sightings.
Distances between camps are deceptive on corrugated roads; fuel and water planning matter more here than daily kilometre targets.
The mountain sits inside the tiny Cape Floristic Region, one of the world’s six recognised floral kingdoms.
Platteklip Gorge is the most direct walking route to the top, but its stone staircase is steep and largely exposed.
Cloud and strong wind can close the cableway quickly — never assume a cable-car descent will be available after hiking up.
Cape Point is dramatic, but it is not Africa’s southernmost tip — that title belongs to Cape Agulhas.
The Flying Dutchman funicular removes most of the climb to the old lighthouse, while the coastal paths deliver the quieter views.
Chacma baboons actively search cars and bags for food; feeding them is dangerous and prohibited.
Boulders protects an endangered land-based colony of African penguins inside suburban Simon’s Town.
The section contains three beaches, three boardwalks and one main penguin-viewing area.
Penguins may cross the visitor paths, but they are wild birds with sharp beaks — keep space and never block their route to the sea.
Nelson Mandela spent 18 of his 27 prison years on Robben Island.
Standard visits combine a ferry, an island bus circuit and a prison tour commonly led by a former political prisoner.
The island became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999 for its layered history of imprisonment and resistance.
Southern right whales are usually the headline visitors from roughly June to November, though timing varies each year.
The cliff path strings together kilometres of elevated shore viewpoints, making land-based whale watching genuinely viable.
Hermanus has a whale crier who signals sightings with a kelp horn — a local tradition rather than a tourist-app notification.
The five-day, 42-kilometre Otter Trail starts at Storms River Mouth and ends at Nature’s Valley.
A short forest walk leads to the famous suspension bridges; the trail can continue steeply to a plateau lookout.
Kayak-and-lilo trips enter the Storms River gorge from the sea, revealing cliffs hidden from the road and hiking paths.
Addo now reaches from semi-arid interior to a marine protected area, allowing it to market a ‘Big Seven’ that includes whales and great white sharks.
The wider park crosses five of South Africa’s nine terrestrial biomes.
The flightless dung beetle has right of way: signs ask drivers not to crush beetles or drive over elephant dung.
iSimangaliso became South Africa’s first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1999.
Lake St Lucia supports hippos and crocodiles beside a mosaic of dunes, wetlands, savanna and coastal forest.
Loggerhead and leatherback turtles nest on the northern beaches in summer, with guided night outings operating in season.
The reserve traces its protected status to 1895, making it one of Africa’s oldest formally proclaimed conservation areas.
Its white-rhino recovery work became a foundation for moving rhinos to reserves around the world.
Beyond game drives, the iMfolozi wilderness area is known for guided multi-day trails where no permanent accommodation is used.
Durban’s subtropical Indian Ocean makes winter beach days far more plausible than they are around Cape Town.
Bunny chow — curry served inside a hollowed loaf — grew from the city’s Indian-South African food culture.
The beachfront is only one layer: Victoria Street Market, the Indian Quarter and KwaMuhle Museum tell a richer city story.
Vilakazi Street is associated with two Nobel Peace Prize laureates: Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu.
The Hector Pieterson Museum places the 1976 student uprising in the streets where it happened.
The painted Orlando Towers are former power-station cooling towers repurposed as a giant urban landmark and adventure venue.
The wider fossil landscape contains dozens of caves and has yielded an extraordinary record of early hominins.
Sterkfontein is linked to both ‘Mrs Ples’ and the unusually complete Australopithecus skeleton known as Little Foot.
Maropeng is the interpretation centre; the fossil caves and museum are separate experiences, so check what a ticket actually includes.
Three Rondavels, Bourke’s Luck Potholes and God’s Window are separate stops spread along the Panorama Route.
The canyon’s subtropical vegetation gives it a distinctly greener character than most of the world’s major canyons.
Low cloud can erase the famous escarpment views; keeping the itinerary flexible is often more useful than arriving early at a fixed time.
The reserve occupies the eroded remains of an ancient alkaline volcanic complex, visible in its concentric ridges.
It is malaria-free and supports the Big Five, making it a popular safari add-on from Johannesburg.
Public roads, picnic areas and hides make independent self-driving practical; sunrise and late afternoon remain the productive windows.
Operation Phoenix moved more than 8,000 animals into the reserve during one of Africa’s largest wildlife reintroductions.
Madikwe is particularly valued for African wild dogs, a species that can be difficult to encounter elsewhere.
This is primarily a lodge-based reserve rather than a casual public self-drive park; game activities are normally arranged by the accommodation.
The pass climbs through tight gravel switchbacks to the Lesotho border at roughly 2,876 metres.
The South African side is a border road, so carry a passport even if your outing feels like a scenic day drive.
Weather can transform the upper road rapidly; snow, ice and summer storms matter more than the conditions down in Underberg.
The park takes its name from the warm evening light on its golden and ochre sandstone cliffs.
Brandwag Buttress is the signature short climb, while longer routes cross open grassland where zebra and black wildebeest roam.
A Basotho Cultural Village and fossil interpretation add useful context beyond the scenic driving loops.
Wolfberg Arch and the Maltese Cross are natural sandstone landmarks reached on separate permit-controlled hikes.
The range protects the endemic Clanwilliam cedar and elusive Cape leopards, though leopard sightings are exceptionally rare.
Exposed trails become punishing in summer; water sources are unreliable and route permits should be arranged before setting out.
The Orange River drops about 56 metres into an 18-kilometre granite gorge at the main falls.
The Khoekhoe name is commonly translated as ‘place of great noise’, especially apt when the river is in flood.
Moon Rock, Ararat and Oranjekom reveal a broader desert landscape that most quick waterfall stops miss.
Mapungubwe was the centre of a powerful southern African kingdom between roughly AD 900 and 1300.
The tiny gold rhinoceros found here became an icon of the site’s sophisticated trade and metalworking culture.
At the confluence viewpoint, the Limpopo and Shashe rivers meet beside the borders of South Africa, Botswana and Zimbabwe.
The famous flower display is usually strongest in late winter and early spring, but rain and temperature decide the exact timing.
Flowers generally face the sun, so late morning to mid-afternoon often produces a better show than dawn.
Skilpad is the accessible flower hub; reaching remote coastal sections is a different trip and may require a 4×4.
The Amphitheatre is a vast basalt wall roughly five kilometres long, with the Tugela River falling from the escarpment above.
The Tugela Gorge walk approaches the wall from below and is a very different day from the high Sentinel route.
The Sentinel chain ladders start from a separate high trailhead outside the main Royal Natal camp area.
Didima Rock Art Centre interprets San imagery and beliefs before visitors encounter the mountain shelters themselves.
Cathedral Peak rises above 3,000 metres and its summit route is a long, exposed undertaking rather than a casual viewpoint walk.
Rainbow Gorge offers a gentler forest-and-stream alternative when the high peaks are hidden by cloud.
Monk’s Cowl is the gateway to Champagne Castle and Cathkin Peak rather than a single summit attraction.
Blind Man’s Corner links day hikers to the long-distance Contour Path and broad views over Champagne Valley.
Sterkspruit Falls is a short option near camp, useful when storms make the exposed ridges a poor idea.
The Main Caves contain well-preserved San paintings and are normally visited on a scheduled guided walk.
The reserve is a strong place to look for eland on open slopes and bearded vultures above the escarpment.
Its valleys are quieter than the central resort belt, rewarding walkers who stay overnight instead of treating it as a photo stop.
The aquarium is designed around a shipwreck theme, turning tanks and passageways into part of the storytelling.
The complex combines aquarium exhibits, water rides, restaurants and direct access to uShaka Beach.
Animal presentations and feeding times shape the best visit order, so checking the day’s programme beats wandering at random.
The stadium was built for the 2010 FIFA World Cup and its huge arch has become part of Durban’s skyline.
The upper adventure walk reaches a glass-floor viewpoint about 106 metres above the city.
The stadium sits beside the beachfront and major sports venues, making it easy to combine with a long promenade walk.
The red-and-white lighthouse has guided ships past the coast since the 1950s and remains Umhlanga’s visual emblem.
A paved promenade runs between beaches, hotels and the distinctive whalebone-shaped pier.
Continue north toward the lagoon reserve for coastal forest and boardwalks that feel far removed from the resort strip.
Founded in 1849, this is Africa’s oldest surviving botanic garden.
Its cycad collection includes Encephalartos woodii, a species extinct in the wild and known only from cloned male plants.
The garden is also a practical birding and picnic stop, not simply a collection of labelled flower beds.
This region links Ts’ehlanyane’s indigenous woodland with the caves of Liphofung and the high road over Moteng Pass.
Bearded and Cape vultures use the mountain cliffs, while rare berg bamboo survives in protected river valleys.
Winter snow and black ice can cut routes that look straightforward on a map; build slack into any cross-highlands drive.
Katse’s 185-metre arch dam is the engineering centrepiece of the Lesotho Highlands Water Project.
The nearby botanical garden covers 17 hectares and preserves indigenous plants rescued during dam construction.
Bokong begins a 32-kilometre, two-to-three-day high-level trek to Ts’ehlanyane National Park.
Thabana Ntlenyana reaches 3,482 metres, the highest summit in southern Africa.
Sehlabathebe’s 6,500 hectares form the Lesotho half of the transnational Maloti–Drakensberg World Heritage Site.
Sani Top sits at an international border, so passport formalities are part of an outing even when the scenery feels continuous.
The Senqu–Orange River begins in Lesotho and runs about 2,200 kilometres to the Atlantic.
Quthing combines dinosaur trackways with missionary and war-era sites rather than being only a fuel stop.
Lake Letsie is Lesotho’s sole Ramsar wetland and one of the region’s richest high-altitude birding sites.
The lowlands route connects six main towns and can be driven in an ordinary roadworthy car.
Thaba Bosiu is both a royal burial place and the stronghold around which the Basotho nation formed.
Morija preserves early mission architecture, archives and one of the country’s deepest collections of historical material.
Maletsunyane Falls drops 192 metres into a gorge close to Semonkong.
Pony trekking here is working transport turned travel experience, often linking villages unreachable by ordinary cars.
Malealea and Semonkong both support community guides, so a guided outing directly connects the landscape with local livelihoods.
The Basotho Hat building is shaped like a mokorotlo, the woven hat that also appears on Lesotho’s flag.
Maseru sits beside the Caledon River and South African border, making border traffic part of everyday city life.
The capital is the sensible place to buy specialist supplies and cash before remote highland circuits.
King Moshoeshoe I established his mountain stronghold here in 1824, and the site became the nucleus of the Basotho nation.
The plateau holds royal graves and remains a place of spiritual importance for traditional healers and seers.
Its name means ‘mountain at night’, tied to the legend that the fortress grew after dark and shrank by day.
Morija became Lesotho’s first major mission settlement in the 1830s and remains a centre of publishing and education history.
The museum’s collections range from Basotho culture and colonial records to fossils and dinosaur material.
Nearby Maeder House dates to 1843 and now gives contemporary Basotho artists a place to exhibit and sell work.
Families still inhabit distinctive mud-and-stone dwellings built beneath a sandstone overhang.
The settlement dates to the early nineteenth century, when communities sought protection during regional upheaval.
A community guide turns the visit from architectural sightseeing into a conversation about a living home and its etiquette.
The rock shelter preserves San paintings of people, eland and hunting scenes above the Liphiring River.
Reaching the art involves descending into the valley, so the walk back is the harder half of the visit.
A local guide helps distinguish faint original pigment from mineral stains and later marks on the rock.
The Maletsunyane plunges 192 metres in a single drop, throwing up the spray that gave Semonkong its ‘place of smoke’ name.
A pony-and-guide outing is a traditional way to reach viewpoints beyond the standard roadside side of the gorge.
The waterfall changes character dramatically with rainfall; the safest viewpoints still require care around unfenced edges.
Semonkong means ‘place of smoke’, referring to spray rising from nearby Maletsunyane Falls.
The town is a launch point for pony treks, village stays, hiking and one of the world’s most dramatic commercial abseils.
Market days and ordinary village life are part of the appeal; the waterfall is not the only reason to leave the lodge grounds.
Malealea helped turn the hardy Basotho pony into one of Lesotho’s best-known community tourism experiences.
Routes range from short rides to multi-day journeys reaching rock art, waterfalls and remote villages.
The local band and village walks are not staged add-ons: they help distribute visitor income beyond accommodation.
This high pass is the dramatic western approach to Malealea, opening suddenly onto layers of sandstone mountains.
The best photographs often come from stopping before the final descent rather than from the settlement below.
Mist can replace the famous panorama within minutes, so treat the viewpoint as a weather-dependent bonus.
The park is the world’s most important stronghold for endemic berg bamboo, which gives Ts’ehlanyane its name.
More than 20 mammal species occur here, with eland and rock hyrax among the most conspicuous.
Its trail network ranges from waterfall walks to horseback routes and the multi-day high traverse from Bokong.
The broad sandstone overhang preserves San rock art as well as evidence of later Basotho use.
King Moshoeshoe I is traditionally said to have sheltered here while travelling through the northern highlands.
The cultural centre adds Basotho history and craft context to a site that would otherwise look like a simple cave stop.
A 32-kilometre trail crosses the alpine plateau from Bokong to Ts’ehlanyane over two or three days.
Cape vultures breed on cliffs opposite the visitor centre; grey rhebok are often seen running across the grassland.
Most day visitors only walk to Lepaqoa Falls, but hiking is permitted much more widely with weather awareness and local guidance.
The double-curvature concrete arch wall rises 185 metres and can be explored on an organised engineering tour.
Katse stores water for transfer toward South Africa as part of a much larger tunnel and hydropower system.
Boat trips reveal the reservoir’s scale better than the roadside overlooks and reach steep valleys hidden from the dam wall.
The 17-hectare garden was created to rescue and propagate indigenous plants affected by the Katse project.
Its collections emphasise Lesotho’s medicinal, ornamental and useful plants rather than imported display species.
Birdlife and short paths make it an easy counterpoint to the concrete-and-turbines engineering tour next door.
The resort sits above 3,000 metres and relies heavily on snowmaking during its short winter ski season.
Outside winter, the same slopes switch to hiking, mountain biking and high-altitude training.
Altitude, wind and sun exposure can surprise visitors arriving directly from the South African lowlands.
Moteng is the paved gateway between Butha-Buthe and the high Oxbow–AfriSki corridor.
The pass gains altitude through tight bends with views into deeply cut Maloti valleys.
Winter black ice and rockfall are more consequential than 4×4 capability; check conditions before committing to the crossing.
The border post sits around 2,876 metres above a staircase of switchbacks descending into South Africa.
Sani Top is a settlement and trekking base, not only the location of the famous ‘highest pub’ photo.
From here, guides lead long high-altitude walks toward Thabana Ntlenyana and shepherd settlements beyond the road.
At 3,482 metres, Thabana Ntlenyana is the highest point in Lesotho and all of southern Africa.
The normal approach crosses broad, poorly marked highland terrain rather than following a built summit trail.
Clear mornings can become stormy afternoons quickly; a local guide is valuable even though the slopes are not technical.
Established in 1970, Sehlabathebe was Lesotho’s first national park.
Its 6,500 hectares protect rock pools, sandstone formations and species found nowhere outside the Maloti–Drakensberg system.
The park forms the Lesotho component of a transboundary UNESCO site shared with South Africa’s uKhahlamba Drakensberg Park.
The protected trackway contains dinosaur footprints estimated at about 230 million years old.
Quthing has several fossil-track sites; the small roofed display is the easiest one to inspect without a long hike.
A craft shop shares the site, making the stop as much a community visit as a palaeontology exhibit.
Missionary David-Frédéric Ellenberger built the cave house into a sandstone overhang in 1866.
Inside is an eccentric stone piano as well as material on missionary life and local palaeontology.
The wider Quthing route also contains dinosaur tracks and British–Baphuthi conflict sites, so the museum makes more sense in context.
Mohale’s reservoir sends water through a 32-kilometre interconnecting tunnel toward Katse.
A small cruiser operates on the reservoir and can reach Thaba-Chitja Island when conditions and schedules allow.
The approach road is itself an engineering landscape of high passes, cuttings and enormous mountain views.
Ribaneng is reached on foot or pony through rural valleys rather than from a developed viewing platform.
The waterfall is most impressive after summer rain, while the approach can become muddier and river crossings harder.
A village guide is useful for access etiquette and route-finding because paths divide repeatedly between settlements and fields.
Lake Letsie is Lesotho’s largest natural freshwater body and the centrepiece of its only Ramsar wetland.
The lake sits above 3,000 metres in an 800-hectare grassland basin visited by blue cranes, vultures and highland endemics.
There is no accommodation or restaurant at the lake; the rough final roads and picnic-style visit reward full self-sufficiency.
